It occurred to me that while I may explore quite a bit, and occasionally my family will as well, there is no good way to communicate points in space for various areas. I am familiar with maps from a military career and even for familiar terrain, we used maps alot in the field. I use maps alot when I explore, but it's on my phone and I can't depend on that for more than 24 hours.

I ordered a topo map from mytopo.com to see if it's useable. Does anyone have opinions on maps from there? Reviews seem to be generally positive for them. Perhaps recommendations for other map sources?

It's been more than 10 years since I ordered stuff from mytopo.com but they were pretty solid if I remember right.

Here are a couple of other options from the US Geologic Survey:

http://nationalmap.gov/ustopo/index.html

http://nationalmap.gov/historical/

I'm not sure if they are what you are looking for but they are at least free. Although the historic maps will be at least 7 years old, they have been field inspected (I think) and if you are in an area without much development they should be fairly accurate.
Please follow up with your thoughts on the map. I've been trying to find a decent topo map.

Large scale map data is freely available from the USGS and probably your own government as well, if you want to make your own maps with GIS software.

QGIS is decent and free and can handle most data formats.

QGIS is nice. If you look at Plugins like QuickMapServices or OpenLayerPlugins you can find some topo data. For example in Quick Map Services you can access ASTER GDEM contour data. It's not great resolution but may be useful.

A company called Raven Maps in Medford, Oregon makes some very high-quality large topo-maps for entire states (I'm not affiliated with them except as a happy customer). I think the elevation shading is a lot easier to read than the USGS styling, but because the maps are quite large they are not necessarily good for field-use or prepping.

http://www.ravenmaps.com

What I do is go to the local library/kinkos and use the plotter to print out a map from this site: http://viewer.nationalmap.gov/basic/?basemap=b1&category=ustopo&title=US%20Topo%20Download

Other than that, you can get topo shapefiles from a google search, and can create your own maps in arcgis/qgis.

Of course, I recommend having a laminated copy, even though they can be harder to read. They will last a lot longer.
